They mention only that some drums have a strap mount so that the instrument can be played standing or while dancing, and that a thin stick, called çubuk in Turkish (meaning stick or rod), is used for striking. Beyond those part names and their uses the sources give no materials, and no information on the material of the body or the head.

演奏時可將鼓夾於腋下、置於腿上，或側放膝上；有背帶者也可站立或邊舞邊打。初學先以: When playing, you can tuck the drum under your arm, rest it on your legs, or lay it on its side across the knees; with a strap you can also play standing or while dancing. A beginner starts by striking the centre of the head with fingertips and palm for a lower, more open sound, then strikes near the rim with the fingertips for a higher sound, and the other hand on the rim gives another high note. To close the sound, press the hand briefly on the head. The Egyptian-style rim is more rounded, which helps fast rolls; the Turkish-style rim stands proud, which makes finger snaps and other fine techniques easier but works against fast rolls. More advanced practice includes slaps, strokes on the body, and moving the fist in and out of the flared opening to change the timbre.

達布卡鼓常見於北非、中東與巴爾幹傳統音樂，也見於南亞、東歐傳統音樂；在蘇拉威西作: The darbuka is common in the traditional music of North Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans, and also appears in that of South Asia and eastern Europe; in Sulawesi a large goblet drum is set on the ground and played as a temple instrument. Middle Eastern folk and modern music and dance rhythms are often built on it. In Western classical scoring Berlioz uses a tarbuka in the fourth act of Les Troyens, and Halim El-Dabh wrote Fantasia-Tahmeel for goblet drum and string orchestra, premiered in New York in 1958 with Stokowski conducting.
達布卡鼓為單面膜鳴鼓，鼓身呈高腳杯形，H-S 編號 211.26。演奏者通常將鼓: The darbuka is a single-headed membranophone with a goblet-shaped body, H-S number 211.26. Players usually tuck the drum under the arm or rest it on the legs and strike it lightly with the fingertips and the palm; it can also be laid on its side across the knees, or fitted with a strap and played standing or dancing. It is common in the traditional music of North Africa, the Middle East and the Balkans, and appears too in that of South Asia and eastern Europe; in Sulawesi a large goblet drum serves as a temple instrument.
達布卡鼓為單面膜鳴，輕柔指尖與手掌敲擊產生共鳴而延音較短。鼓面中心以指掌擊出較低: The darbuka is a single-headed membranophone: light strikes with fingertips and palm set the head resonating, and the sustain is fairly short. The centre of the head, struck with fingers and palm, gives the lower “doom”; the rim, struck with the fingertips, gives the higher “tak”; the other hand gives “ka”; and pressing the hand briefly on the head gives the closed “pa”. Players move the hand in and out of the opening to change the timbre, damp the head, and may also slap or strike the side of the drum. The rounded Egyptian rim helps fast rolls; the exposed Turkish rim makes finger snaps easy, but its hard edge works against fast rolls.
達布卡鼓為杯形單面膜鳴鼓，古代美索不達米亞與埃及文化已有使用，巴比倫與蘇美早至公: The darbuka is a goblet-shaped single-headed membranophone already in use in the ancient cultures of Mesopotamia and Egypt, with traces in Babylonia and Sumer as early as 1100 BCE; the large goblet drums of Sulawesi, played on the ground, may reflect an ancient usage. Its name comes from Egyptian rural Arabic, from a word meaning “to strike”. The drum spread through North Africa, the Middle East, the Balkans, South Asia and eastern Europe, and developed into the rounded-rim Egyptian and the exposed-rim Turkish types. In the 1950s the Egyptian-American musician Halim El-Dabh wrote for goblet drum and orchestra, and his Fantasia-Tahmeel was premiered in New York in 1958; an earlier Western classical use is in Hector Berlioz's opera Les Troyens (1856–1858).
